paras: The bombing of the Gertrude Harrison residence was a pair of bomb attacks in May 1919 on the home of Mrs. Gertrude Harrison, a Black resident of 4807 Grand boulevard in Chicago, Illinois. The second bomb, around May 29, damaged only a skylight and two back windows, and no arrest was reported. The Black press carried the story as part of a run of bombings of Black homes in the city, and the Chicago Defender blamed the police for a perfunctory investigation.

The Associated Negro Press described the house as a "beautiful residence" in "one of the exclusive sections of Chicago," and called the family "among Chicago's most highly respected people." The Defender placed it in a police district "where considerable bomb throwing occurred recently." Who owned the house is unclear: a garbled Defender passage says the property was "purchased outright," while later Defender items say attorney William B. Austin owned it and Mrs. Harrison occupied it.

According to the Defender, the first bomb was thrown about two weeks before the second; it was "alleged" that a man got out of a yellow taxi and planted it in the vestibule. The second bomb, which a Chicago dispatch dated May 30 placed on the previous day, was set off from the roof of the adjoining house rather than in a hall or vestibule. Onlookers told the Defender they could not see how the bombers reached that roof without using the neighboring building's fire escape.

The explosion destroyed a skylight and two back windows, and no one is reported hurt. The Defender judged that the bomb was meant more to intimidate than to destroy, since a larger charge would have damaged the adjoining property.

Police from the fourth precinct arrived an hour after the explosion, asked the occupants a few questions and left, and the Defender wrote that "that is where the investigation ended." Mrs. Harrison told the paper that the bombing had not frightened her and that she would remain at 4807 Grand boulevard permanently. No report of an arrest appears in the coverage.

In June the Defender reported that Austin had been told by an anonymous caller to "get rid of the Colored people" in the house, and that his own home on Bellevue place was then attacked; the paper's two items give different nights and house numbers. One item says bombers placed dynamite under his basement and did much damage, and that Austin vowed to pursue the bombers and "the higher-ups behind them." Alderman Louis B. Anderson was reported in touch with the police and pointed to the "Kenwood improvement Association," formed for "keeping undesirable people out of the community."

The Chicago Defender broke the story on its front page on May 31 under "Home of Mrs.Gertrude Harrison Target for Bomb Throwers," with the subhead "Lazy Police Blamed." Its report also passed on rumors that Jewish real-estate speculators stood behind the bombings, though it added that this did not apply where the property had been bought outright. The Baltimore Afro-American ran a two-line brief, "BOMB CHICAGO HOME," on June 6.

An Associated Negro Press dispatch carried the story more widely, appearing in the Omaha Monitor on June 5, the St. Louis Argus on June 6, and the Dallas Express, Phoenix Tribune and Savannah Tribune on June 7. Headlines ranged from "CHICAGO RESIDENCE IS TWICE BOMBED" to "STILL BOMBING COLORED HOMES" and "CONTINUE TO BOMB HOMES OF NEGROES." The longer wire text called the bombings "infamous acts," relayed a claim that neighbors had planned the bombing, asked why police had not brought the bombers to justice, and warned that one of the most serious riots the city had known could follow.
By June 21 the Defender treated the case as one of a wave of bombings, quoting white supporters such as Edgar A. Bancroft, who called the bomb throwing "wholly un-American."

The Defender's first report gives the address as 4507 Grand boulevard, but its own continuation and every other report give 4807. The perpetrators were never identified in the coverage: the wire relayed a claim that neighbors planned the attack, and the Defender reported rumors of real-estate speculators.

reader.title: Bombing of the Gertrude Harrison residence
bases: Unidentified bombers twice bombed a Black family's residence, damaging the building but injuring no one (A1, A2, A5).
The Defender's local report (A1, A2) agrees with a separate Chicago brief in the Afro-American (A5) and the Associated Negro Press wire (A4, A6) on a second bombing within two weeks.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender local report
accounts.gist: Bomb thrown from the roof of the adjoining house, the second in two weeks; police came an hour later, asked a few questions and left; Mrs. Harrison said she would stay.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press wire
accounts.gist: Bombers had for a second time in two weeks bombed the beautiful residence of a highly respected family in an exclusive section; some claimed neighbors planned it; police had failed to run down the bombers.

accounts.label: William B. Austin (via Defender)
accounts.gist: The owner said he had been told by an anonymous caller to get rid of the Colored occupants, and his own home was then attacked.

record_check.dossier: Second bombing about May 29, 1919 (dispatch of May 30 says 'yesterday'); the first about two weeks earlier.
4807 Grand boulevard in every report but one Defender passage.
Black: the owner was told to remove 'the Colored people' from the house; wire headlines speak of 'COLORED HOMES'.
Mrs. Gertrude Harrison and her family; the June 21 Defender calls her Mrs. Richard B. Harrison.
At least nine articles in seven Black papers, including the ANA wire and Defender follow-ups on June 21.
No arrest is reported; the Defender says police came an hour later, asked a few questions and left.

info: Second bombing on about May 29, 1919 ('yesterday' in a May 30 Chicago dispatch); first about two weeks earlier, in mid-May.
Residence of Mrs. Gertrude Harrison, 4807 Grand boulevard, Chicago (4507 in one Defender passage).
Mrs. Gertrude Harrison and her family, occupants of the house; also named Mrs. Richard B. Harrison.
Unidentified 'bomb throwers'; some claimed neighbors planned it; rumors of Jewish real-estate speculators.
